title: The Anointing, the King's Entry, and the Hour
summary: Six days before Passover Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume, and Jesus defends her against Judas, saying she has kept it for his burial. The next day crowds welcome him into Jerusalem with palm branches as the King of Israel, and when some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified, like a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. The chapter closes John's account of Jesus' public ministry with a reflection on unbelief drawn from Isaiah and Jesus' final public appeal.
story:
Chapter 12 is the hinge of John's Gospel. The first half, often called the Book of Signs (the name Raymond Brown used in his commentary of 1966), has shown Jesus revealing himself through a series of signs, usually counted as seven, and the discourses that interpret them. The second half, which Brown called the Book of Glory, will tell of his last evening with the disciples, his death, and his resurrection. Throughout the first half Jesus has said that his hour had not yet come (2:4, 7:30, 8:20). Now, when Greeks come asking for him, he says “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23).

The raising of Lazarus in chapter 11 set everything in motion. It drew crowds to Jesus and led the council under the high priest Caiaphas to resolve that he must die (11:47-53). Jesus withdrew to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness (11:54), and pilgrims arriving early for Passover wondered whether he would dare come to the feast (11:55-57). Chapter 12 answers: he comes, openly, first to a dinner in his friends' home and then into the city as a king. The chapter sets two responses side by side, extravagant love and royal welcome on one hand, calculation, betrayal, and unbelief on the other. It ends with Jesus hiding himself (12:36), the narrator's verdict on a people who saw the signs and did not believe (12:37-43), and a last summary of everything Jesus has said in public (12:44-50). After this he speaks only to his own.
historical:
John dates the dinner “Six days before the Passover” (12:1). In John's reckoning the Passover lambs were slaughtered on the afternoon Jesus died, a Friday (19:14, 19:31), so six days earlier falls around the Sabbath, and the entry into Jerusalem comes the next day (12:12), the first day of the week. The church's Palm Sunday rests on this reckoning together with the order of events in the other Gospels. Bethany lay about fifteen stadia, a little under two miles, from Jerusalem (11:18), on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives along the road to Jericho. The modern Arab town there is called al-Eizariya, a name that preserves Lazarus. Mark and Matthew also tell of an anointing at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, and place it two days before Passover (Mark 14:1-9, Matthew 26:6-13); how these accounts relate is taken up among the hard questions below.

Passover brought Jews from across the Roman and Parthian world to Jerusalem. Josephus reports that when the Roman governor of Syria, Cestius Gallus, had the priests count the lambs at a Passover in the 60s AD, they numbered 256,500, and he reckons a crowd of more than two and a half million (Jewish War 6.422-427). Historians treat these figures as greatly inflated, but the city certainly swelled many times over. The festival remembered Israel's liberation from Egypt, and under Roman rule it could stir hopes of another liberation. The governor normally came up from Caesarea with extra troops, and Josephus describes soldiers posted on the roofs of the temple porticoes at Passover to watch the crowds, a practice that led to a deadly riot under the governor Cumanus around AD 48 to 52 (Jewish War 2.224-227, Antiquities 20.106-112). Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, and Caiaphas held the high priesthood from about AD 18 to 36. A crowd hailing a Galilean as King of Israel in the city at Passover was exactly what the priests had feared when they said the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation (11:48).

Palm branches had become a symbol of national triumph. When Simon Maccabeus took the citadel of Jerusalem from its Seleucid garrison in 141 BC, the people entered it with praise and palm branches, harps, cymbals, and hymns (1 Maccabees 13:51), and when Judas Maccabeus purified the temple around 164 BC the worshipers carried palm fronds (2 Maccabees 10:7). Palm trees and the lulav, the festal bundle of palm, myrtle, and willow, later appeared on coins struck by the Jewish rebels against Rome, most famously in the Bar Kokhba revolt of AD 132 to 135. Only John specifies that the crowd's branches were palms; Mark speaks of leafy branches cut in the fields (Mark 11:8).

The Greeks of verse 20 are Hellēnes, Gentiles, not Greek-speaking Jews (whom Acts 6:1 calls Hellenists). They had come up to worship at the feast, which marks them as God-fearers, Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without becoming Jews, like the centurion Cornelius (Acts 10:2). They could enter the great outer court of the temple, but a stone balustrade barred them from the inner courts, with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who went further would be responsible for his own death (Josephus, Jewish War 5.193-194, Antiquities 15.417; m. Middot 2:3). A complete copy of the Greek inscription was found in Jerusalem by Charles Clermont-Ganneau in 1871 and is now in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum. The Greeks approach Philip, and Philip goes to Andrew; both disciples have Greek names and came from Bethsaida (1:44), a town just east of the Jordan in the territory of Herod Philip, who refounded it as Julias (Josephus, Antiquities 18.28).

Verse 42 says that many of the leaders believed but would not confess it for fear of being put out of the synagogue (aposynagōgos, also at 9:22 and 16:2). J. Louis Martyn's History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel (1968) argued that these passages reflect the experience of John's own community late in the first century, and linked them to the Birkat ha-Minim, a benediction against heretics in the synagogue's daily prayer. Later scholars, among them Reuven Kimelman (1981) and Jonathan Bernier (Aposynagōgos and the Historical Jesus in John, 2013), have argued that the benediction's date and target are too uncertain to carry that weight and that local exclusion of Jesus' followers during his lifetime is historically plausible. What the text itself shows is a leadership divided, with belief present among the rulers but held in silence.
cultural:
The dinner at Bethany is a deipnon, the main evening meal, at which guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched away from the table. That posture explains how Mary could reach Jesus' feet. Martha serves (diēkonei), as she does in Luke 10:38-42. Mary's perfume was a litra of nard, a Roman pound of about 327 grams or eleven and a half ounces, which the BSB renders about a pint. Nard was an aromatic oil from a plant of the Himalayan highlands, Nardostachys jatamansi, carried to the Mediterranean through India at great cost. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s AD, says that the spike of nard sold for up to a hundred denarii a pound (Natural History, book 12), and a prepared perfume cost more. The adjective pistikos is uncertain: it may mean genuine or pure, unadulterated nard, or it may derive from a place or plant name now lost. Judas values the perfume at three hundred denarii; since a denarius was a laborer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2), that is roughly a year's income once Sabbaths and feast days are subtracted.

Anointing a guest's head was a familiar honor (Psalm 23:5, Luke 7:46). Anointing the feet was not; feet were the lowest and dirtiest part of the body, and washing them was a servant's task. To wipe them with her hair Mary must have let her hair down, which a respectable woman did not ordinarily do before men who were not her family; the Mishnah counts a wife going out with her hair unbound among offenses against Jewish custom (m. Ketubbot 7:6). John does not comment on the impropriety. He notes only that the house was filled with the fragrance. Anointing a body for burial was a normal act of love (Mark 16:1), so important that the Mishnah permits anointing and washing a corpse even on the Sabbath (m. Shabbat 23:5). Jesus reads Mary's act as that last service performed in advance. The contrast with 19:39 is deliberate: one litra poured on the living Jesus by Mary, and some hundred litrai of myrrh and aloes brought by Nicodemus for his body.

Almsgiving belonged to Passover. The Mishnah requires that even the poorest Israelite receive four cups of wine at the Passover meal, from the charity fund if necessary (m. Pesahim 10:1), and when Judas leaves the supper the disciples assume Jesus has sent him to give something to the poor (13:29). Judas's objection therefore sounded pious. John adds that Judas kept the common purse (glōssokomon, a box or case) and helped himself; the verb bastazō means to carry, and in the right context to carry off, and John may intend the pun. Jesus' reply, that the poor will always be with them, echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, whose point is not resignation but a command to open one's hand to the needy brother.

The next day the crowd goes out to meet Jesus (eis hypantēsin), a phrase used in Greek for the formal civic welcome of an arriving dignitary, when citizens went outside the walls to escort him in. Their cry comes from Psalm 118:25-26. Hosanna transliterates the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, ‘save, please’. Psalm 118 closes the Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118), which Levites sang while the Passover lambs were slaughtered (m. Pesahim 5:7) and families sang around the Passover table (m. Pesahim 10:6-7); at the feast of Tabernacles worshipers shook the lulav at the words of 118:25 (m. Sukkah 3:9). Pilgrims knew the words by heart, and the psalm's blessing on him who comes in the Lord's name was a welcome to pilgrims that the crowd now turns into an acclamation of the King of Israel, the title Nathanael gave Jesus at the beginning (1:49). Jesus answers with a symbol of his own. Kings of Israel rode mules and donkeys in peace (1 Kings 1:33-38, where Solomon rides David's mule to his anointing), and Zechariah 9:9 pictured Zion's king coming righteous and humble on a donkey's colt, not on a war horse.

The images in Jesus' speech were familiar. A seed that dies in the ground to produce grain is a farmer's picture, and Paul uses it for the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:36-38). To love and hate one's life is a Semitic way of expressing preference, as when Leah is said to be hated because Jacob loved Rachel more (Genesis 29:30-31); Luke 14:26 and Matthew 10:37 show the same idiom and its meaning. A voice from heaven that some took for thunder recalls Sinai, where God answered Moses in thunder (Exodus 19:19), and later rabbinic tradition spoke of the bat qol, a heavenly voice that spoke after prophecy had ceased (b. Sanhedrin 11a). The phrase sons of light (12:36) was also used at Qumran, where the community's Rule opens by calling its members to love all the sons of light and hate all the sons of darkness (1QS 1:9-10), and the War Scroll (1QM) describes a final battle between them. Jesus uses the image without the hatred: the light is among them, and they are invited to believe in it while they can.
literary:
The chapter has three scenes and two closing reflections. The anointing (12:1-11) and the entry (12:12-19) are both royal acts, since kings were anointed and welcomed in procession, but the first points to burial and the second to a humble king. Each ends with the chief priests or the Pharisees reacting (12:10-11, 12:19), and both turn on Lazarus, whose raising brings the crowds. The coming of the Greeks (12:20-36) triggers the turning point of the Gospel, marked by the word hour (12:23, 12:27) and by Jesus' troubled prayer, which reads like John's counterpart to Gethsemane in the other Gospels (Mark 14:32-42): the troubled soul, the prayer about the hour, the submission to the Father's will. Here the struggle is compressed into a question he raises and answers himself.

John writes with pointed irony. The Pharisees complain that the whole world (kosmos) has gone after Jesus (12:19), and the very next verse brings Greeks to see him. Judas speaks for the poor while robbing the purse. The crowd hears the Father's voice and thinks it thundered. The narrator also lets the reader know more than the characters. He explains that the disciples understood the entry only after Jesus was glorified (12:16, as at 2:22), and that the saying about being lifted up indicated the kind of death Jesus would die (12:33), a remark he repeats when that death comes (18:32).

The verb lifted up (hypsoō) is one of John's double meanings. It appears in three sayings (3:14, 8:28, 12:32) that function like the three passion predictions in the Synoptic Gospels (Mark 8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34), and it means both raised up physically on a cross and exalted to glory. The same double sense lies behind glorify: the hour of shame is the hour of glory.

The narrator's reflection (12:37-43) sets two Isaiah texts side by side, 53:1 (who has believed our message?) and 6:10 (the blinding and hardening), and the early church used both to explain unbelief (Romans 10:16 quotes Isaiah 53:1; Mark 4:12 and Acts 28:26-27 use Isaiah 6:9-10). The link between them is deliberate. Isaiah 6:1 sees the Lord high and lifted up, and Isaiah 52:13 uses the same pair of Hebrew words for the servant who will be lifted up and exalted. By adding that Isaiah saw his glory (12:41), John joins the vision of the enthroned Lord to the suffering and exalted servant and applies both to Jesus.

The final speech (12:44-50) has no setting. Jesus has just hidden himself (12:36), and yet he cries out. It reads as a closing summary of his public teaching, gathering the themes of the first half: believing, seeing, sending, light and darkness, judgment, the Father's command, and eternal life.

outline.t: The Greeks come; the grain of wheat
The troubled soul and the voice from heaven
Unbelief and the prophecy of Isaiah

doctrines.note: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23). In John the Son's glory is revealed supremely in his death and exaltation, and the Father answers his prayer with “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (12:28). The chapter also says that Isaiah saw Jesus' glory (12:41), identifying the glory of the enthroned Lord of Isaiah 6 with Jesus.

“Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed” (12:24). Jesus' death is the way to a harvest of life for many, including the nations. When he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself (12:32), and in the same hour the ruler of this world is cast out (12:31): the cross is both a gift of life and a victory over evil.

The crowd hails Jesus with Psalm 118 as the King of Israel, and he accepts the title but enacts Zechariah 9:9, entering as a humble king on a donkey. The crowd's objection that the Christ remains forever (12:34) shows the collision between the expectation of an unending reign and a Messiah who must be lifted up in death. His kingship will be proclaimed over the cross (19:19).

John says of the unbelievers that “they were unable to believe” and cites Isaiah's words about blinded eyes (12:39-40), while holding them responsible, describing leaders who believed but would not confess, and ending with Jesus' continued appeal (12:44-50). The chapter holds God's purpose and human responsibility together without explaining how they fit; see the hard questions.

The arrival of the Greeks signals that Jesus' death will open the way for the nations, and his answer speaks of much fruit (12:24) and of drawing everyone (12:32). The Pharisees' complaint that the whole world has gone after him (12:19) is truer than they know. The disciple's mission follows the same pattern: to serve Jesus is to follow him where he goes (12:26).

words.note: Doxazō, to glorify, to honor, to reveal the glory of. It occurs about 61 times in the New Testament and 23 times in John, more than in any other book, and five times in this chapter (12:16, 12:23, and three times in 12:28). In ordinary Greek it meant to hold an opinion of or to praise, but in the Greek Old Testament it took on the sense of God's weighty, visible presence. In John, Jesus is glorified above all in his death, resurrection, and return to the Father, which turns the world's idea of glory upside down: the place of shame is where God's glory is shown.

Hōra, hour. It occurs about 106 times in the New Testament and 26 times in John. It can mean a time of day, but in Jesus' phrase my hour it means the appointed time of his death and glorification. It had not yet come at Cana (2:4) or at the feast of Tabernacles (7:30, 8:20). Here it arrives (12:23), and Jesus refuses to pray to be saved from it (12:27). From now on the Gospel speaks of the hour as present (13:1, 17:1).

Hypsoō, to lift up or exalt. It occurs 20 times in the New Testament and five times in John (3:14 twice, 8:28, 12:32, 12:34). John uses it with a double meaning: Jesus will be lifted up physically on a cross, which is why the narrator adds that he was indicating the kind of death he would die (12:33), and he will be lifted up in exaltation. Isaiah 52:13 in the Greek Old Testament uses this verb with doxazō for the servant who will be lifted up and glorified, and the crowd's question in 12:34 shows they heard the word as a reference to death.

Helkyō, to draw or drag. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, five of them in John: the Father draws people to the Son (6:44), the lifted-up Son draws everyone to himself (12:32), Peter draws his sword (18:10), and the disciples drag the net full of fish (21:6, 21:11). BDAG notes its range from physical hauling to moral or spiritual attraction. The word does not by itself settle debates about whether grace can be resisted, but in 12:32 it pairs with everyone (pantas) to stress the universal reach of the cross: not Jews only but Greeks as well.

Psychē, life or soul. It occurs about 103 times in the New Testament. It can mean physical life, the self, or the inner person, and this chapter uses both senses in quick succession. Whoever loves his life (psychē) will lose it (12:25), and two verses later Jesus says that his own soul (psychē) is troubled (12:27). The one who asks his followers to let go of their lives is himself shaken at the cost of letting go of his, which keeps the demand from being cold.

Pōroō, to harden, make dull or insensitive. It occurs five times in the New Testament (Mark 6:52, 8:17; John 12:40; Romans 11:7; 2 Corinthians 3:14), always of hearts or minds that fail to perceive. In quoting Isaiah 6:10, John does not follow the Greek Old Testament, which uses a different verb and a passive, the heart of this people has grown dull. His wording, with a verb in the active voice (he has hardened), stands closer to the Hebrew, where the prophet is told to make the people's heart fat, and it presents the hardening as God's judgment.

Aposynagōgos, put out of the synagogue, excluded from the community. The word occurs only three times in the New Testament, all in John (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and it is not known from any earlier Greek writing. It names a real social cost: exclusion from the synagogue meant separation from family, worship, and village life. Its use here explains why believing leaders stayed silent, and verse 43 names the deeper reason, that they loved human glory more than God's glory, a play on doxa.

Entaphiasmos, preparation for burial, the laying out of a body. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here (12:7) and in Mark's parallel account (Mark 14:8). The word shows that Jesus reads Mary's act in the light of his coming death, whether or not she fully understood it. It also ties the anointing to 19:40, where Jesus' body is wrapped with spices according to Jewish burial custom (entaphiazein, the related verb).

christ:
Jesus enters Jerusalem as the king Zechariah promised, humble and bringing salvation, and the crowd sings Psalm 118 over him, the psalm of the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). John shortens Zechariah's oracle and opens it with “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion” (12:15), words that may echo Zephaniah 3:14-16 or Isaiah 40:9, where Zion is told not to fear because the Lord her king is in her midst. The effect is to present the arrival of Jesus as the arrival of Israel's God as king.

The chapter shows that this kingship comes through death. Mary anoints Jesus as kings were anointed, but for burial. He is the grain of wheat that falls into the ground, the Son of Man lifted up, the servant of Isaiah 53 whose message was not believed. When John adds that Isaiah said these things “because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him” (12:41), he identifies the Lord whom Isaiah saw enthroned, high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1), with Jesus. The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah already renders 6:1 as seeing the glory of the Lord, and John may be drawing on that way of reading. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) has argued that John places Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God precisely at the point of his humiliation: the servant who is lifted up in death shares the throne of the Lord who is high and lifted up.

The voice from heaven (12:28) is one of three in the Gospel tradition, alongside the baptism (Mark 1:11) and the transfiguration (Mark 9:7). Here it answers the Son's prayer that the Father's name be glorified, and it is spoken for the crowd's sake (12:30). The hour of the cross is also the hour of judgment on the world and the casting out of its ruler (12:31), a claim the Gospel repeats at 16:11. Jesus' death is not a defeat that must later be reversed but itself the victory, which the resurrection vindicates.

The chapter also shows the humanity of Christ. His soul is troubled (12:27), the same verb John uses of his distress at Lazarus's tomb (11:33) and at the betrayal (13:21). He goes to the cross as a real man, afraid, and yet willing, refusing to ask to be spared from the hour for which he came. And his last public words show him as the one sent: whoever believes in him believes in the Father who sent him, whoever sees him sees the one who sent him (12:44-45), and he came not to judge the world but to save it (12:47).
interpretation:
Jewish tradition read Zechariah 9:9 messianically. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets it beside Daniel 7:13 and records the saying that if Israel is worthy the Messiah will come with the clouds of heaven, and if not, poor and riding on a donkey; Rashi's commentary on Zechariah refers the verse to the King Messiah. Psalm 118 remained part of the Hallel sung at Passover and the festivals, so Jewish readers have always heard the crowd's words as festal liturgy. The Targum of Isaiah's rendering of 6:1 as a vision of the glory of the Lord, and its recasting of 6:9-10 so that the prophet describes a people who do not understand rather than causing their blindness, are traced in Craig Evans, To See and Not Perceive (1989), which surveys how early Jews and Christians wrestled with Isaiah's hardening oracle.

Among the fathers, Augustine's Tractates on John 50 to 54 cover the chapter. In Tractate 53 he answers the question why they could not believe by saying, in effect, because they would not: God foresaw their evil will and announced it through the prophet. John Chrysostom (Homily 68 on John) argued that the word because in 12:39 marks the outcome, not the cause: Isaiah did not make them disbelieve; he spoke because they were going to disbelieve. Gregory the Great, in a homily of 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 33), identified Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary Magdalene, a fusion that shaped Western preaching and art for more than a thousand years. The Eastern churches kept the three women distinct. The Roman calendar revised in 1969 separated Mary Magdalene's feast from the penitent of Luke 7, and in 2021 Pope Francis made 29 July the memorial of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus together.

The entry shaped Christian worship early. The pilgrim Egeria, visiting Jerusalem around 381 to 384, describes the people gathering on the Mount of Olives on the Sunday before Easter, hearing the Gospel of the entry, and escorting the bishop down into the city with palm and olive branches and the cry of Psalm 118. The procession spread west, and Theodulf of Orléans wrote Gloria, laus et honor (All glory, laud, and honor) for it in the early ninth century. The crowd's words, joined to Isaiah's Holy, holy, holy, became the Sanctus and Benedictus of the eucharistic liturgy. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 12:12-16 at the Liturgy of the Palms in Year B, 12:20-33 on the fifth Sunday in Lent in Year B, and 12:1-8 on the fifth Sunday in Lent in Year C.

Calvin's commentary on 12:39-40 held that God blinds as a just judgment on those already rebellious, so that the fault remains theirs, and the passage was cited on all sides in later debates over predestination. Modern scholarship has concentrated on three questions: the chapter's place as the close of the Book of Signs (Raymond Brown's Anchor Bible commentary, 1966 and 1970); the setting of the synagogue expulsion passages (J. Louis Martyn, 1968, and his critics); and John's christology of glory (Bauckham, 2008). Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz have asked Christian readers to notice how 12:37-43 has been heard as a verdict on Jews as such, when John himself records that many believed (12:11, 12:42).

The grain of wheat has had a long afterlife. Fyodor Dostoevsky set 12:24 as the epigraph of The Brothers Karamazov (1880), where it frames the elder Zosima's teaching and the novel's account of suffering that bears fruit. The Greeks' request in 12:21, in the King James wording ‘Sir, we would see Jesus’, has often been placed inside pulpits where only the preacher can read it. In art, Giotto painted the entry in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1305), and Duccio included it in the Maestà for Siena Cathedral (1308 to 1311).
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 1 the later Byzantine text, followed by the King James Version, adds that Lazarus was the one who had died (‘which had been dead’); the earliest manuscripts lack it. In verse 7 the best manuscripts read a purpose clause, literally ‘Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial’ (as in the ESV), which raises the question of how she could keep what she had just poured out; answers include that she kept the rest, or that she has kept it until now for this purpose. Later manuscripts smoothed this to a perfect tense, ‘against the day of my burying hath she kept this’ (KJV), and the BSB's rendering, She has kept this perfume, gives that sense. In verse 17 most manuscripts say the crowd that was with him when (hote) he called Lazarus kept testifying, but some early manuscripts read that (hoti), making the crowd testify that he had called Lazarus from the tomb. In verse 32 nearly all manuscripts read everyone (pantas, masculine plural), but Codex Bezae and the Latin Vulgate read all things (panta; Latin omnia), a reading that gave Western theology a picture of the cross drawing the whole creation to Christ. In verse 41 the best manuscripts say Isaiah spoke because (hoti) he saw his glory, while the later text reads when (hote), the King James Version's ‘when he saw his glory’. In verse 47 the best text says the one who hears and does not keep (phylaxē) Jesus' words; the later text reads does not believe (KJV ‘believe not’).

The Old Testament quotations also differ from the Greek Old Testament. Verse 15 abbreviates Zechariah 9:9 and replaces its opening call to rejoice with an assurance not to fear. Verse 38 follows the Greek of Isaiah 53:1 exactly, including the address Lord, which is absent from the Hebrew. Verse 40 departs from both the Hebrew and the Greek of Isaiah 6:10: it drops the ears, reorders the clauses, and makes God the one who blinds and hardens, where the Greek has a passive. The adjective pistikos in verse 3 is rendered pure (BSB, ESV), genuine, or spikenard (KJV); its exact meaning is uncertain.

teach.big: The hour of Jesus' glory is the hour of his death, and the love that pours itself out for him, the faith that follows him into death, and the confession that costs something are the right responses to a king who reigns from a cross.

outline.t: Extravagant love for Jesus is never waste. Mary gives her best while Judas calculates, and Jesus reads her gift in the light of his burial.
Life from Jesus provokes hostility as well as faith: the living Lazarus is himself evidence that the powers want removed.
Jesus accepts the crowd's praise as King but redefines kingship by riding a donkey, and even the disciples understood only after the resurrection.
The nations' seeking marks the hour. Fruitfulness comes only through dying, for Jesus first and then for those who follow him.
Jesus is honestly troubled and still chooses the hour. The cross is where the Father's name is glorified, the world is judged, and all kinds of people are drawn to him.
The light is present for a limited time, and the right response to Jesus is to believe while the light is here.
Unbelief in the face of the signs was foreseen in Scripture, and it also has a human face: people who love human approval more than God's.
To receive Jesus is to receive the Father who sent him; he came to save the world, and his word will be the standard on the last day.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first uses 12:8, the poor you will always have with you, as a reason to shrug at poverty or to justify spending on churches instead of the needy. Jesus is echoing Deuteronomy 15:11, which commands generosity because poverty will persist, and he is speaking of a unique moment before his death; the Gospel itself assumes the disciples gave to the poor (13:29). The second merges Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary Magdalene, and preaches Mary's act as a prostitute's repentance. John names her as Lazarus's sister and says nothing of that kind.

The third preaches Palm Sunday as the fickle crowd that shouted Hosanna and days later Crucify him. John does not say the same people did both, and the crowd that came from Bethany was bearing witness to what it had seen. The fourth takes the hardening of 12:39-40 as fatalism, telling hearers that some people simply cannot believe and so need not be invited. John follows the quotation immediately with leaders who did believe and with Jesus' continued public appeal. The fifth hears 12:37-43 as a verdict on Jewish people. The passage concerns the response of particular people in Jesus' day, and the chapter repeatedly notes Jews who believed (12:11, 12:42).

Finally, hating one's life in this world (12:25) is not a call to self-contempt or to neglect of the body. It is a Semitic way of saying prefer, and it describes a disciple who holds even life itself loosely compared with following Jesus.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on the grieving. The grain of wheat is read at many funerals, and it can comfort, but a grieving person should not be told that their loss was needed so that something good could grow. Jesus speaks of his own chosen death, not of every death. His own troubled soul (12:27) gives permission for fear and distress in the face of death; teach that Jesus did not pretend. Those who feel they cannot believe, or who fear that their doubts mean God has hardened them, may hear 12:39-40 as a sentence. Point them to the fact that John sets it alongside people who came to faith and a Jesus who keeps calling. The saying about hating one's life should never be taught in a way that a person who is depressed or thinking of self-harm could take as permission; name that clearly and keep the way to help open. Those who keep their faith quiet for fear of losing family or work (12:42-43) deserve both honesty and compassion, especially where confession carries real danger.

hard.q: If God blinded their eyes so that they could not believe, how can they be blamed?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. John says “For this reason they were unable to believe” (12:39) and then quotes Isaiah in a form that makes God the one who blinds and hardens. Read plainly, that seems to make God the cause of unbelief and then to condemn the unbeliever for it. Desiderius Erasmus pressed this kind of objection in On the Freedom of the Will (1524), arguing that the Bible's texts on divine hardening must describe God's permission or his patience, since a God who causes sin and then punishes it would be unjust. Jewish readers have raised a further concern: Adele Reinhartz and others have noted that Christian preaching often turned this passage into a theological explanation of why Jews as a people did not believe, with grave consequences in later history.

The main responses differ in how much weight they give to divine action. Augustine (Tractates on John 53) answered that they could not believe because they would not; God foresaw their evil will and the prophet announced it. John Chrysostom (Homily 68 on John) read because as marking the outcome foretold, not its cause. Martin Luther, answering Erasmus in The Bondage of the Will (1525), and John Calvin in his commentary held that God truly hardens, but as a just judgment on hearts already turned from him, so that the guilt remains human. Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress that in Isaiah the hardening follows long refusal and that the gospel's light hardens those who resist it, so that inability is the consequence of prior unwillingness. Craig Evans (To See and Not Perceive, 1989) showed that Jewish interpreters, from the Aramaic Targum onward, and early Christians alike struggled with the harshness of Isaiah 6:9-10 and softened or explained it in different ways.

What all these readings share is John's own framing. His main concern is to assure his readers that the widespread rejection of Jesus did not take God by surprise; Scripture had foreseen it. He immediately adds that many leaders did believe (12:42) and that Jesus went on pleading with people to believe (12:44-50). How God's purpose and human responsibility fit together is a question on which faithful Christians in the Augustinian, Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, and Wesleyan traditions still differ, and John leaves both truths standing.

hard.q: Is John's anointing at Bethany the same event as the anointings in Mark and Luke, and why do the details differ?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. Mark and Matthew place an anointing at Bethany two days before Passover in the house of Simon the leper, where an unnamed woman pours nard on Jesus' head and unnamed disciples object (Mark 14:1-9, Matthew 26:6-13). John places it six days before Passover, apparently in the home of Lazarus and his sisters, names the woman as Mary and the objector as Judas, and has her anoint Jesus' feet and wipe them with her hair. Luke tells of a sinful woman in Galilee, at the house of a Pharisee named Simon, who weeps on Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them (Luke 7:36-50). David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) and many critical scholars after him have treated all of these as variations of a single remembered event reshaped in the telling, and they point out that the wiping of feet with hair makes more sense in Luke, where it wipes away tears, than in John, where it wipes away perfume.

Others distinguish two events. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.79) held that Luke's story is an earlier and different occasion and that Matthew, Mark, and John describe the same later anointing at Bethany, though he also thought the same Mary acted on both occasions. Many modern commentators, among them D. A. Carson (1991) and Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of John's Gospel, 2001), likewise separate Luke's account from the Bethany account, and harmonize Mark and John by noting that Mark's placement may be topical, framing the plot against Jesus, and that a woman could have anointed both head and feet. Some think details from the two events influenced each other in oral retelling.

On any view the four Gospels agree on the heart of the scene: a woman's costly devotion, an objection about money, and Jesus' defense of her. Mark and John also agree that Jesus interpreted it as preparation for his burial. How the details are to be harmonized is a question on which careful readers differ.

observe: What does Mary do, what does Judas say about it, and how does Jesus interpret her act (12:3-8)?
What do the crowd shout as Jesus enters Jerusalem, and what Scripture does John say the donkey fulfilled (12:13-15)?
What reason does verse 43 give for the silence of the leaders who believed?
interpret: Why does the arrival of some Greeks lead Jesus to say that the hour has come, and how does the grain of wheat explain his answer?
What does Jesus mean by being lifted up from the earth, and why does John explain it (12:32-33)?
How can John say both that they were unable to believe and that many of the leaders believed?
apply: Judas called Mary's gift a waste. What would it look like for your love for Jesus to seem extravagant to others?
What in your life might need to fall into the ground and die so that something can bear fruit?
Where does the desire for approval shape what you are willing to say about your faith?
